# Voice and tone

How the product speaks: the words in every component.

## The five answers

| Question | Answer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which kinds of copy does it need? | Labels, messages and articles | Articles are the product; the UI copy must match them. |
| How many tones does it use? | One per moment | Warm by default, calmer for errors. |
| How is the voice defined? | Principles and examples | Editors work from principles and examples, not word lists. |
| How does it sound? | Conversational | Talk to one reader, like a good editor. |
| Where do the words matter most? | Articles and guides | Most words are in articles and guides. |

## When to use what

| Situation | Use | Not | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A button label | A warm verb a reader would say | "Submit" or "Click here" | Buttons are part of the reading voice. Example: “Subscribe” |
| The words of an error | Calm and helpful. Take the blame, offer the way forward. | Blaming the reader | A calm error keeps the reader's trust. Example: “We could not save your email. Check it and try again.” |
| A success message | Warm and brief, with what happens next | A bare "Done" | A warm close invites the reader back. Example: “You're in. The next issue arrives on Friday.” |
| An empty state | An invitation, not a dead end | "No items" | An empty list is a chance to show what the product offers. Example: “Nothing saved yet. Tap Save on any article to read it later.” |
| A confirmation question | Gentle and clear about what changes | Guilt or pressure | Readers come back when leaving felt respectful. Example: “Unsubscribe from the weekly letter? You can come back any time.” |
| A first visit | One sentence on what is here and why it is worth reading | A sign-up wall | Occasional readers decide in seconds whether to stay. Example: “Practical guides, one a week. Start with the most read.” |
